title: 2026/08/27 - EN (Part 2 of 2)
machineSummary: NZ Fish and Game Council said the bill threatens hunting access, noting $20 million spent on wetlands. EDS said the bill requires amendments to prioritize conservation. ESEG, representing Mercury and Meridian, said 60% of electricity relies on DOC land, urging easement protection for the Waitaki Power Scheme.

chunks.text: Amendment Bill. And our first submitter this afternoon is New Zealand Fish and Game Council. Welcome, Carina. How's it going? Kia ora. Good. Nice to be here. Thank you. You've got 15 minutes with us, so take your submission as read- Mm-hmm... uh, and we'll hand it over to you to open up, and then we'll open up for questions.

Oh, thank you very much. I've just got a, um, a short opening statement and, and then I'll leave plenty of time for questions. Um, kia ora koutou, and thank you for the opportunity to speak today. My name's Carina Jordan, and I am the chief executive of the New Zealand Fish and Game Council. Um, I've spoken to you all before, so, uh, I know that you know who Fish and Game is. Statutory manager for sports fish and game birds, established under the Conservation Act 1987. And we represent around about 175,000 license holders, anglers, and

game bird hunters. So firstly, Fish and Game agrees that the conservation framework needs to be modernized, and we welcome the move to a more integrated and efficient system. Obviously, this is where our statutory functions sit under the Conservation Act, uh, so this is a process, um, that is highly relevant to the organization and top of mind, um, for us at the moment, while we're also thinking about further changes to the Wildlife Act and also consideration of a fish and game bill on the future horizon.

The points I want to raise today are points we think may not have been fully worked through as the bill was put together, rather than objections to what the bill is trying to achieve. And so we're hoping our submission was seen in that light and that has been helpful. And we look forward to continuing to work, um, with the government, um, with the Minister for Conservation, and with the Department of Conservation, um, on, uh, as the planning framework is established through the National Conservation Policy Statement and

area plans. Just a couple of points. Angling and game bird hunting value should be recognized as distinct from recreation. I set this out in quite a bit of detail within our submission. This is really important because parts of the proposed changes to the Conservation Act are significantly, um, uh, walk across or step across Fish and Game statutory, current statutory functions, the values of sports fish and game birds, and our activities on the conservation estate. And so we think some material changes are really required to

be made through the Amendment Bill to ensure that those statutory functions are retained and those powers are retained by the organization. Uh, we're seeking an amendment to Section 6A and Section 6EA to recognize hunting and fishing values as standalone values, and I set that out in more detail. We're not recognized as partners in the new planning framework.

I've a little bit of alluded to that at the beginning. It doesn't, um, through the framework, it enables the, uh, Minister for Conservation to make decisions, but there's no requirement to essentially consult with Fish and Game in relation to our values or the management of sports fish or game bird, uh, populations through the provisions of the bill. And this is further weakened by the way that our, our, um, management plans, our sports fish and game bird management plans are treated by the amendments through the bill as well.

So they become subservient to the higher level policies within the Conservation Amendment, um, framework without recognizing fishing or game bird hunting values as standalone values in themselves. The other one that we want to talk about is that our statutory functions shouldn't require a concession. So we undertake game bird, um, monitoring and sports fish monitoring within the conservation estate.

Things like electric fishing, um, looking at spawning surveys, and also management over game bird populations, and we're wanting those to be exempted from, uh, the requirement to have a concession. So in closing, we support the bill as it's been set up to do. Uh, us, a practical refinements that would make the framework work better for our anglers and our hunters, um, and for the fisheries wetlands and access they depend upon. And recognizing hunting and fishuring, fishing as distinct values bring our management plans into the framework and make us a consul tee rather than

as an afterthought, I think will strengthen up the management of their species and their habitats. Brilliant. Thank you very much. Um, we will go first to Ryan Hamilton for a question. Thanks, Carina. Um, is your concern that this bill removes existing rights and responsibilities, or that it fails to explicitly provide for them in the proposed?

We think it weakens them by the changes that have been made. We don't think that that's obviously intentional. We think it's just a, a function of the amendments that have been put forward. Okay. Thank you. And Grant. Yeah. Just this one, um, the last point you made about exempting you from the concession process. So, um, if you were, how would you... Obviously, there's still gotta be a relationship with DOC and gotta work with them. Um, how, how, how would you envisage that would happen and, you know, so that they don't get surprised if you're working and things in a space, you

know? It would, uh, be undertaken as sort of it is, is at the moment where we can, um, we engage directly with the DOC regional offices- Yeah... um, and essentially have a relationship with them whereby we can go in and undertake those activities. They understand when we're in the conservation state undertaking those activities, so it avoids, uh, conflict.

Hmm. Okay. I might just jump in and ask a question. Because obviously, you get a lot of international visitors coming through and fishing in the rivers, et cetera. And obviously, that takes its toll on the DOC land and huts and tracks and everything. Are you supportive of being able to look at more development, I suppose, on DOC land, and obviously, the international visitor levy being able to use to be put back into work on the huts and tracks and upkeeping a lot of the DOC estate?

Yes, definitely. What we know is that we need to invest in the DOC estate to be able to manage it. The taxpayer money only goes so far. Hmm So looking at other economic opportunities for the conservation estate just makes sense. I think our point of view is just that we should be consulted if it's to do with excess of hunting and fishing or hunting and fishing values and the management of those areas in relation to those values.

So that's our predominant ask. But essentially, trying to create revenue and economic benefit from the conservation estate makes sense to put that money back into conservation. Can I just supplement? Yes, go for it, Raj. I was reading about your sports fish game management plans. Yes It's a new term for me.

Can you provide examples where they've provided or delivered environmental outcomes that may not have otherwise been? Because I know it was similar, we talked before about the HOSI, but is that a parallel, or can you give some evidence of where those plans have actually enhanced environmental outcomes? Yes. So, it's a little bit of a combination.

Wetlands are probably the one that comes immediately to mind. So we've put about $20 million back into wetland restoration and enhancement across New Zealand. So that's not only just on the... It's partly in the conservation estate, but mostly outside of the conservation estate. But that's one clear example about how- Right... implementation of our functions and the additional license holder contribution can be implemented on the ground in relation to habitat restoration.

Okay. Thank you. Yes, up on that as well. You talk about here, concessions and visitor amenity areas must assess effects on hunting, angling, habitat, and access. I'm just curious as to the access one, I think it's reasonably self-explanatory, but in terms of the impact on the other issues, what sort of impacts are you potentially seeing that will be created from visitor amenity areas?

Well, our main concern there is just to make sure that the hunting and fishing values are recognized when considering visitor amenity areas and how they will be managed and the relative impact that will have on existing hunting and fishing. I think an example I've got is just, for example, when we're thinking about changing land designations, stewardship land comes to mind.

Mm-hmm. The hunting and freshwater fishing values were supposed to be recognized, and they were recognized to a certain extent. But they weren't carried through to the re-designation of that land. And so, through that process, we actually lost access and lost a number of those hunting and fishing areas because of that land designation. So our concern really is just that if you're changing the way that land is considered or land is to be managed, then please consider the hunting and fishing values and access to them in any management frameworks.

Brilliant. You've got another one, Grant. I might just jump in- There you go... quickly. The 26 that you talk about here, do you want to just elaborate a little bit on that? Because you've said that that is the most important provision, and it's relatable to Fish and Game, but we haven't had any other submissions yet that have raised that specific point, so.

Yeah. Have you got what page are you looking at? So I'm just on page two. It's 26Q1. Basically, where you're making some recommendations around that. I'm just wondering whether... I just don't quite understand that particular recommendation that you're making.

Yeah. I'm just grabbing our detailed submission. Because you talk about it, but I'm just wondering what your- You're asking... what you're specifically asking there to be actually changed within the legislation itself. Just because obviously that's quite unique and specific to Fish and Game.

Helen, do you want to jump on there while I grab it? Oh, Helen- She's grabbing it too... you're just on mute there. There we go. I'm just looking it up in the table at the end, Carina. Oh, is there a table? I don't think we've got a table. No. 26Q functions of fishing.

Yeah. At the end of the submission, page 47, there's a table with suggested changes, amendments. Oh, I'm not sure I got that on my- We've only got a four-pager. We've got 13 pages. No, the full submission is 59 pages. Oh, that explains. Oh, okay. We were not given that submission.

So we've got a detailed appendix which sets out clause by clause the specific changes that we're wanting to make to the provisions. Okay. We can recirculate that. Do you want to send that perhaps through to us? Because we've only got- I've only got 13 the short. We've got a 13-page submission.

Summary. That says- But 26Q was about the functions of Fishing Game Council. Yes. What was the submission about around that? Yeah. We might need to get that thorough full submission that obviously we don't have. But we've got the summary. Sorry, I can't find it in the table.

That's okay. If you want to come back to us on that. That was just- I should be able to-... a particular main area that you wanted us to address within the legislation, so that's why I was just keen to understand a little bit more about it Yeah. I'll try and do that off the top of my head with that, but we'll circulate. You should have the detailed submission in front of you, so we'll make sure that that gets pre-circulated to you.

But essentially, the main thing is the linking Fish and Game statutory functions under Section 26 of the Conservation Act through to the Amendment Bill. And so the main ones, as I was talking about, is recognizing sports, fishing, game birds- Yeah... their habitats, and then the role of Fish and Game in managing them. So that's sort of at a nutshell, which is the main point of the submission.

Yeah, so to make sure that's transferred over to- Yes... and recognizes that within the Amendment Bill. Yes, that's right. And carried right through. So, I can give you it clause by clause, but it talks to a number of amendments-... through the proposed changes to the Conservation Act. Okay. No, that's helpful. Thank you. Grant? Yeah, just a question I want to raise with you.

Obviously, there was a lot of discussion, controversy around the whole concept of the sale and swapping of land. Have you guys got a strong view on that? I'm just-- Where did Fish and Game sit on that whole concept of DoP being able to sell or swap land?

I appreciate that this has been a fraught topic. I've seen it play out through social media. Our position is that we're not opposed to disposals at all. We understand that there is a need for the Department of Conservation to be able to exchange or dispose land. Mm. Our main concern is that if disposals are being considered, that access to hunting and fishing areas are retained in consideration of those disposals.

So, that's the main concern we're hearing from our hunters and our anglers. The primary issue for hunting and angling is still access- Mm... and it is retained as access. Yeah. Just very brief sup on that, because for you, it's more about the process of making sure that the process would include consulting with the groups that you represent, basically.

That's right. One of the amendments that we've sought is for the Minister for Conservation to consult with Fish and Game in considering our values, how those values are treated, and also if disposals are being considered. And then we can talk to the minister or talk to the Department of Conservation about the values, the level of those values, where there are high values or what, and then what is required to retain those values. Often it's access, but access can be provided for through disposals like, for example, using esplanade reserves or

strips. Yeah. So it's often not just the area of the land, but if you take that land out, then it's the access through that land to a resource- Mm... that's a major issue. Yeah. Fish and Game's been successful in doing that. Yeah. Yes. So we have. So we've got a great example of that that's been run by the Auckland-Waikato Fish and Game Council, where they bought a piece of land to put an enduring access to a resource, and then the idea being that as they sell that land back off, retaining that access for current and

future generations. Yeah, I was going to ask for an example, but you've obviously- Yes... just given a good example of- Mm. And we think that's a great blueprint for the future as well, and it means that hunters and anglers are actually putting in access not only for them, but also for our wider community, and it's funded by the license holder. Absolutely. Brilliant. Hey, thank you very much for your- That's great... submission today. Appreciate you coming in in person as well.

And, yes, we will fish out the find the pun, the full submission, and work out what's happened there potentially. It's swimming around somewhere. Swimming around somewhere. Hey, thank you very much, Karina. Appreciate your time today and your thorough submission there.

Thanks. So, we now welcome through our next submission for today, the Environmental Defense Society, and they are going to be joining us via Zoom, I understand. So we will just wait for them to pop up. There we go. Shaye, we can see you. Welcome to the select committee this afternoon.

You have 15 minutes with us. We have read your submission. It is a very thorough submission, so do take it as read, and we'll hand over to you to open up and then open for questions. Thank you. Good afternoon, Madam Chair and members of the committee. Thank you for providing EDS with this opportunity to present today.

My name is Shaye Schlaefer. I'm EDS's Chief Operating Officer and General Counsel. I want to start by saying that EDS is opposed to the bill in its current form, but we believe it can be fixed. The bill is not beyond repair. We think that amending the bill and panel beating it into shape would be a better outcome than binning it altogether.

Conservation law reform is required. However, we have several big-ticket issues with the bill that need amendment before we can support it, and these are outlined in our submission, and I address four of them today. We've chosen not to focus on exchange and disposals, because the minister has already said that those provisions should be pulled. So, the first issue I want to discuss is the economic opportunities clauses, and that's new Section 6EA, which has been discussed a lot with other submitters. But also the corresponding

sections in 13D2, 13H2B, and in Section 14, relating to the purpose of the National Conservation Policy Statement, area plans, and the concessions framework. Our first preference is that these clauses be deleted. Alternatively, we have provided some acceptable redrafting in our submission.

Key here is to delete the words "to the greatest extent practicable," and make references to use and development consistent with conservation. And I've watched all of the other submitters who have presented to you to date, and it seems that is a universal request.

Without those changes, the economic clauses place use and development before conservation. And that is because DOC functions have no hierarchy which prioritize conservation imperatives. The words "to enable use and development to the greatest extent practical" are an open-ended maximizing direction, and because there is no corresponding conservation direction in those other clauses I just referred to, to counter the economic purpose of the conservation policy statement area plans and the

concessions framework. Cabinet was very clear that economic development was to be provided only to the extent that it is consistent with conservation. We want to make it clear that does not mean balancing conservation and economic development.

A balancing approach was expressly discounted as an option by Cabinet. So we're simply asking the select committee to give effect to Cabinet's direction to prioritize conservation. The second issue is with visitor amenity areas. EDS supports VAA's in principle as a strategic tool for managing visitors.

However, as drafted, the VAA framework under the bill is not consistent with conservation. And that is reflected in a few different places. The purpose statement for visitor amenity areas, the broad list of activities that are provided for, that visitor amenity areas operate as an override of area plans, and the conservation purpose for which the land is held, that the assessment of VAAs is focused on the parent land, which has the potential of minimizing impacts that are actually significant at the estate scale, and finally, that public input on the development of VAAs is

limited. So in that context, we have considerable concern with the minister's decision-making powers for VAAs. There are simply not enough conservation guardrails to ensure that the minister's decisions on VAAs is required to prioritize conservation values and imperatives.

And we've set out in our submission the amendments that we think are required to the VAA framework to bring it into an acceptable position. The third issue I want to highlight is the centralization of decision-making power with the minister and the corresponding reduction in the roles of the Conservation Authority and conservation boards.

EDS does not think that streamlining the conservation system requires removing those checks and balances. The Conservation Authority provides independent national level expertise and oversight, and conservation boards bring local knowledge and provide an important connection between conservation decision making and the communities that are affected by it.

So under the bill, those roles are significantly diminished while the minister assumes greater control over conservation management planning. And that is particularly concerning when combined with the economic development imperative and the broad VAA powers that I've just discussed. Those changes all pull in the same direction, which is greater scope for development, coupled with fewer independent and place-based checks on how those powers are exercised.

We support streamlining the planning system, but streamlining should mean removing unnecessary complexity and delay, not removing conservation guardrails. We therefore recommend retaining a meaningful decision-making role for the Conservation Authority and conservation boards within the new planning framework.

And the final issue I want to address relates to climate change. So the bill is silent on climate change considerations, and that has also flowed through into the conservation policy, the first draft of that. And we think that is a significant omission for a law that is intended to provide a new framework for managing the conservation estate for decades to come.

Climate change is already affecting conservation management. It's changing where species can survive, it's increasing pressure on vulnerable ecosystems, and it's increasing risks to DOC assets and infrastructure. And I know that one of the members referred to the Cathedral Cove scenario, which is a prime example of this.

So new planning and concession systems need to be able to respond to those changes. We recommend that the bill integrate climate change considerations into the planning and concessions framework. And again, our submission sets out how we recommend that occur. So to sum up, EDS supports reform of the conservation system. There are real problems with the current system, and there is a lot in this bill that provides a good foundation for change.

But the fundamental principle of any new conservation law must remain clear that conservation comes first, and we don't think that the bill as introduced achieves that. We're happy to take questions. Brilliant. Thank you very much, Shay. I've got a question just in relation to conservation boards, because that's been raised quite a bit throughout the submission process. You also raise it in your submission, and you've just touched on the concentration of power with the minister, which obviously concerns you. What's your

specific solution in relation to that? Well, we would like to bring back the decision-making role of the Conservation Authority and the boards that has been stripped out of the bill. Awesome. Yeah. Okay. So, that would be what you would want to see through this process. Grant- Yeah... has a supplementary on that.

I suppose my supplementary is around, so effectively what the design's to do now is they've still got to be consulted with the conservation authority, the boards, and that information is obviously public information was provided through to the minister. Why don't you see that as sufficient?

Given that the minister is ultimately responsible for the decisions that the conservation authorities make. Yes. Well, there are kind of two elements to this. So, the first issue is that the framing of the bill does not put conservation first. So, there is no certainty within that framing that the minister's decisions will prioritize conservation values.

And the second thing that I think has come through quite clearly from other submitters who are much closer to the decision-making process than EDS, like the Conservation Authority, Ngāi Tahu, the tourism operators. What I've heard quite clear from them is the importance of local decision-making in terms of a check on the system and making sure that those decisions actually endure. And so, we would like the framing of the bill to change, and for that community role to be strengthened.

Just- Sup... just a quick sup on that. You say that the framing of the whole bill is not focused on conservation, or words to that effect. Well, actually, the original purpose still sits there in the original title of the original act. It hasn't changed, and that conservation sits at the top. Mm-hmm. So, I'm a bit bemused and confused by that statement.

There is no one single purpose in the Conservation Act, so you have to interpret its purpose by looking at various clauses together, and that includes Section 6, DOC's functions, the definition of conservation. There's a few other things in that mix. The title of the act. But there is no prioritization of those functions.

So yes, while there is still a conservation function in there for DOC, it does not sit above the economic clause. And in fact, the words in those economic opportunities clauses, to the greatest extent practicable, to our mind, actually require DOC to start from a position of needing to grant approval, and instead of considering whether that concession is an appropriate use in the first place.

So, I think it actually switches the whole framework around. Thank you. Celia. Thank you very much. And particularly thank you for giving us the links to your previous documents about tourism and nature and landscape. And I hope because they've been referred to here, we may be able to use them later. But, my particular question, you talk about the role for the NZCA and for the conservation boards, and you talk about commission of inquiry.

What sort of items would you imagine being set as a commission of inquiry by the NZCA? That's a great question, Celia. Anything that is substantive. We've called for commissions of inquiries recently for reviewing the fisheries management system.

We've also had an independent inquiry into land use in Tairāwhiti, so these are the big kind of national level issues that affect the conservation estate in this case. Thank you. Look, we've got time for one last question. Scott. Thank you, Shay.

You've mentioned that we can panel beat this bill into shape. So, do you think if we create the hierarchy with the conservation guardrails at the very top, that is going to be the key? All the other points you've made, but that's really the fundamental issue here, isn't it?

That we need to have a hierarchy with the conservation guardrails. Or is there something else that we need to get right? I think there are three main framing issues that need to be changed in the bill, and you're quite right, the economic opportunities clauses, not just in 6EA, but the subsequential ones as well. That needs to be fixed, and I think you've heard quite clearly, and we have drafting on how you could do that. The visitor amenity framework almost sits as an independent tool above the system. So, that needs to be integrated back into it, and

parts of that need to be tweaked as well to bring conservation to the fore. And I think the final thing would be to elevate that community voice, to make sure that there is that additional check. Brilliant. Thank you very much, Shay, and thank you for your submission and all of the points you've raised.

Really valuable feedback, so we appreciate that going through this process. So, thank you. Thank you So now we move to our next submitter today, Electricity Sector and Environment Group, who are with us in person. Welcome, Martin and team, to the select committee this afternoon, and thank you for also your very thorough submission as well. Do take it as read, but you do have 15 minutes with us. So we'll hand over to you to open up, and then we'll have questions. Thank you.

Thank you, Chair. Good afternoon, members of the committee. Yes, my name's Martin Williams, counsel for the Electricity Sector Environment Group, or ESEG, as we call it. I'm here with Christina Healy, environmental policy manager at Mercury, and Andrew Fairbairn, environmental policy manager at Meridian.

Just to hit the highlights of the written submission, starting with this. Firstly, acknowledging that reform of the Conservation Act is long overdue and is strongly supported. The legislation is outdated, unnecessarily complex, and poorly drafted. Arguably, it's beyond repair or panel beating, and broader reform is needed to align with the RMA reform programme, but that's a story for another day. As matters stand, ESEG supports, in particular, the simplification of the planning system, the national conservation policy statement for all types of conservation land, and a single

layer of area-based plans and secondly, the improvements to the concessions process, fitting time frames for completion, provision for standardized conditions, and exempt or pre-approved status. Great innovations. The Conservation Act planning and concession processes are critical to ensuring an affordable supply of clean energy in New Zealand.

And the government's commitment to doubling the supply of clean, affordable energy under Electrify New Zealand is directly engaged in this context. Little-known fact, breaking news, but as Christina will share with you, some 60% of New Zealand's total electricity generation capacity and output is contingent and utterly reliant on access to the conservation estate.

Oh, wow. With this firmly in mind, ESEG seeks a number of further, but important, changes to the drafting of the bill. Firstly, a new function for the department addressing climate change mitigation and adaptation. This would not only recognize that threatened flora and fauna, along with huts and tracks and visitor facilities, roading are at risk from climate change, but provide the platform for decision making involving renewable electricity generation, or REG assets, on conservation land. It would also, I might add, be better aligned perhaps to the existing departmental functions than

maximizing economic opportunities per se. That's the first thing, new function. Second thing, a form of legal instrument for existing, that's existing, REG assets on the estate, and I'll come to that, and provision for REG activities involving existing assets to be exempt or pre-approved, applying what we'll refer to as the activity cascade, with the concessions process managing the effects around the ongoing operation of the existing assets.

I'll hand over to Christina now to flesh out the point I've just made about 60%, and I think you've got a handout that I'd like you all to have in front of you. We've got maps. Yes, and the maps in particular. Go, Christina. Go, Christina. Thanks, Martin. So I just want to give the committee a sense of the scale of the renewable electricity generation's existing interaction with public conservation land. It's not simply whether or not the power station sits on DOC land. Rather, in practice, it's much more about the generation scheme's reliance on supporting

infrastructure that sits on, under, over, or is accessed through public conservation land. So that might be a tunnel, a canal, a water intake, an electricity cable, or a communications cable, geothermal pipeline, monitoring equipment, or simply an access road or a bridge through public conservation land. It also includes routine activities needed to keep a generation scheme operating safely, access for inspections, maintenance, vegetation management, and replacing aging equipment.

Those supporting activities generally require some form of approval from DOC, usually through the concession system. Sure. The scale of that interaction is significant. The renewable generation assets identified in our submission, which you'll see on the maps in front of you, interact with the conservation estate, are associated with around 26,500 gigawatt hours of electricity each year, about 60% of New Zealand's annual generation.

Wow. Interesting. Mercury's Rotokawa geothermal operations are a really good example. The scheme interacts with public conservation land through geothermal wells, pipelines, transmission, and fiber optic infrastructure, monitoring sites, and access. In one case, we had to apply for a concession for geothermal drilling that passed beneath the Rotokawa conservation area without any surface disturbance on the conservation land.

What may look like a relatively minor concession for access, monitoring a cable or a pipeline, can actually be an important link in the operating arrangements needed to keep an existing generation scheme working safely and reliably. So the key point is, public conservation land and the approvals needed to use it for these supporting activities are already an important dependency for a significant part of New Zealand's renewable electricity supply.

That means secure, workable access to public conservation land is not just an administrative issue for individual generators, it can directly affect the safe and reliable operation of a significant part of New Zealand's electricity system. And Andrew is going to take you through a particular example- Yeah, that'd be good... operating easements.

Good afternoon. Thanks, Christina. The key issue I wish to canvas with you today is the necessity of ensuring the terms and conditions of existing operating easements prevail in cases where crown ownership is moved from LINZ to the Department of Conservation. This is something that is an issue that's in play at the moment, and in EC's view, requires legislative change and the Conservation Amendment Act to provide certainty in the context of the use of those operating easements.

So operating easements, in essence, are instruments that were created at the time respective hydro schemes throughout the country were developed. And provide for maintenance upgrades, ongoing scheme development and lake level management on land the scheme operator doesn't own. I think it's an important point we're going to draw out. EC's position is that the land or subject operating easements should not be transferred into the conservation state unless those easement terms remain fully effective and prevail in any

conflict. Without this protection, conservation management requirements will likely conflict with existing generation rights. The practical risk is delay, constraint, or extra approvals for routine maintenance, upgrades affecting nationally significant renewable electricity infrastructure. And as we speak today, this is particularly relevant in the context of the Waitaki Power Scheme, where transfers are proposed adjacent to Lake Pukaki and the OLC canal, and they're going to be reclassified as Scenic Reserve.

Now, Meridian has been engaging with officials around the need to address this through a legislative fix, but it's fair to say that hasn't been progressed to date. And effectively, I think this is the opportunity that that can be done quite simply. So the proposed solution, the principle I'm really talking about, is really straightforward. Transferring land into the conservation state should not reduce, qualify, or undermine the existing operating easement rights.

The preferred solution is a clear statutory protection confirming existing operating easements prevail over any inconsistent requirement under the Conservation Act, National Conservation Policy Statement, or area plan. And we've provided a solution on Appendix G to our submissions in relation to amendments to, I think, Section 3A of the act.

Alternatively, the bill could provide for a targeted renewable electricity asset instrument, agreed with the operator and approved by the minister, which Martin will talk to shortly. Yeah, just picking up on that. Concessions as a form of approval give you both a property right and their environmental permission. Dealing with the form of the property or the issue, the property right side, concessions are really a poor fit for the type of assets that Christina took you through.

These assets are not like smaller scale, less engineered structures, which the concessions framework was really designed for trades, businesses, occupations of a tourism type nature. Those assets also predate the concessions process. So what's set out in the submission is a bespoke form of property right called a renewable electricity asset instrument, which would be a hybrid lease and easement.

And, and the reason I say the concessions process doesn't work very well is that it's got restrictions on exclusive position, but it's absolutely vital for safety and security. It's got restrictions on the duration of concessions, 30 years, unless exceptional circumstances. These assets last for up to 100 years. Mm. And there's, there's provisions in there where if you're, if you're in the act, even the amended act, if you're in conflict with a single section of the Conservation Act or the NCPS, game over, fatal, can't be

granted. So we're positing a bespoke, um- Yeah... asset, uh, instrument for that purpose. And then sitting aside, alongside that would be the activity cascade that I talked about earlier, where the ongoing management of the assets, uh, and its effects would be provided for under the NCPS.

Generally, whereby ancillary activities would be permitted, in other words, exempt or pre-approved. Um, the, uh, if you didn't adopt that REAI, the, the, um, asset instrument, you would equally, uh, provide for all existing assets, that 60%, to be exempt or pre-approved, and then the concession applications go on and provide for the management and would give direction, uh, the NCPS would need to give direction about whether those applications are notified or not.
